# Compact Language Models with Iterative Text Refinement for Health Dialogue Summarization

Kellen Tan Cheng♠*, Ganesh Ramesh♢*, Nafiul Rashid♣, Geoffrey Jay Tso♣, Jilong Kuang♣

♠Microsoft ♣Samsung Research America ♢Nutanix ♠kellencheng@microsoft.com, ♢ganesh.ramesh@nutanix.com ♣{n.rashid, geoff.tso, jilong.kuang}@samsung.com

## Abstract

Health wellness agents typically rely on large language models (LLMs) for response generation, where contextual information from a user’s conversation history can be used for response grounding and personalization. Highquality conversation summaries are one such method which can reduce the number of input tokens during response generation, decreasing overhead and inference latency. However, directly purposing LLMs for this task is infeasible due to the scale of the task, the compute overhead, and health data compliance regulations. Furthermore, ground truth for real-world datasets is scarce due to privacy concerns and the high cost of health expert annotators. These factors necessitate the development of small, potentially on-device, language models capable of health dialogue summarization, particularly in the absence of ground truth labels. In this paper, we first present a comprehensive empirical study that benchmarks a variety of stateof-the-art smaller language models to better understand their baseline capabilities. Second, we present an unsupervised method that uses the summaries from multiple models, refined with iterative feedback, to generate high-quality summaries of health dialogues. Experiments illustrate that our method is able to outperform baseline on both open-source and proprietary benchmarks. Notably, our method can be run viably on local compute without a GPU, using just a single Macbook with 16 GB of memory.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have spurred the development of health assistants capable of automating clinical workflows, generating diagnoses and advice, outputting userpersonalized responses, acting as voice assistants, summarizing health contexts, and more (Qiu et al., 2024; Abbasian et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a;

Liu and Wang, 2023; Yang et al., 2024b; Singhal et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Cosentino et al., 2024; Mukherjee et al., 2024). For effective health wellness agents, contextual information from prior conversations can be utilized to help ground and personalize the agent’s response to the user. Since appending all prior conversations during response generation can be costly, high-quality conversation summaries can be used to succinctly represent the same information at a lower token cost, reducing memory overhead and response latency. As a result, these summaries are an important component in the development of effective health wellness assistants. Despite the impressive capabilities of state-ofthe-art LLMs, directly adopting them for health conversation summarization presents several challenges. First, these models incur substantial memory compute overhead, and introduce latency and monetary cost considerations with their usage, on top of increased carbon emissions. Second, health data compliance regulations may restrict, or even ban, the ability to send user health information to externally hosted LLMs to perform health dialogue summarization. Such factors raise a potential question: can we perform health conversation summarization without LLMs, using models that can either be ran on-device or hosted locally? Towards this objective, we first benchmark a suite of smaller language models (LMs) to gauge and analyze their baseline capabilities for health dialogue summarization. Instead of blindly selecting a model to use, we evaluate a variety of state-of-theart smaller LMs, ranging from 0.5B up to 4B parameters. We utilize multiple aspects of evaluation, namely both automatic metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR, BERTScore), when applicable, as well as winrate comparisons (Lin, 2004; Papineni et al., 2002; Banerjee and Lavie, 2005; Zhang* et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2023). We also present an approach to generate highquality health dialogue summaries in an unsuper-

More specifically, we extract several agent-generated summaries for a given conversation, before then refining each summary using text feedback in a silo. These refined summaries are then merged together to generate the final output. Our expectation is that through this approach, we can cultivate and refine diverse yet accurate conversation summaries. We tailor our method to various models by benchmarking on differing numbers of agents and rounds, in order to determine the most optimal setting for each model. We then use these settings to run our experiments. For a comparison across multiple settings, we evaluate our results on both open-source benchmarks (Ben Abacha et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2024a) as well as real-world health wellness conversations. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We perform evaluation benchmarking on a suite of smaller LMs for health conversation summarization, ranging from 0.5B to 4B parameters. (2) We present an unsupervised method for summary generation from health conversations. Our approach generates several summaries for each dialogue and iteratively refines these summaries using textual feedback. The final summary is then generated from all the refined summaries. (3) We provide a comprehensive analysis of our summaries, investigating its viability as a ground truth generation method for fine-tuning, as well as a comparison to conventional multiagent debate.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Health Dialogue Summarization

Health and medical dialogue summarization is an important tool to improve the accuracy and personalization of an agent’s responses to a user/patient. This has been studied in the context of generating clinical notes (Yim and Yetisgen, 2021; Michalopoulos et al., 2022), medical topic-based methods (Liu et al., 2024; Nair et al., 2023), synthetic dialogue generation (Chintagunta et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2023), or through the introduction of shared tasks (Ben Abacha et al., 2023a). We study health dialogue summarization through the lens of developing better health wellness assistants. Unlike prior work, we focus particularly on small LMs that can be ran locally, removing the need for LLMs at all. Additionally, our approach does not

require expert annotators or specialized medical domain knowledge.

### 2.2 Summarization From Feedback

Prior work has demonstrated the utility of incorporating feedback to fine-tune and align LMs (Ouyang et al., 2022). Text feedback has shown promise in enhancing model capabilities (Yuan et al., 2024), particularly for summarization (Chen et al., 2024; Fernandes et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Stiennon et al., 2020; Bai et al., 2022). These works typically utilize human annotators for verbose text feedback generation, whereas our proposed method is entirely unsupervised, removing the need for annotators entirely. Furthermore, automatic processes typically utilize LLMs directly and/or incorporate feedback generation during inference (Kirstein et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025), which introduces significant compute overhead. With smaller LMs, our approach can bypass this challenge through our iterative text feedback process, as well as aggregating multiple refined summaries to generate the final output.

### 2.3 Multiagent Frameworks

The adoption of multiagent frameworks in recent years has led to improvements in the text generation and reasoning capabilities of LLMs (Du et al., 2024). Multiagent frameworks incorporating feedback have been utilized towards improving LLM critique quality (Lan et al., 2024; Kargupta et al., 2025), enhancing agent collaboration (Wan et al., 2025), and table refinement (Yu et al., 2025). Concurrent work (Fang et al., 2025) has also demonstrated the viability of these frameworks for text summarization. Unlike true multiagent frameworks, our method iteratively improves agent generated summaries within a silo, removing the inter-agent communication step within each round. We motivate this approach because summarization is inherently subjective, and different viewpoints may summarize the same content differently (Li et al., 2021; Steen and Markert, 2024; Fabbri et al., 2021). In this manner, we aim to model this setting by preserving and refining summaries that may originate from different agents, rather than having all agents converge onto the same summary. This process allows the final output to incorporate information from a variety of refined summaries. Crucially, our approach also differs by focusing on small LMs capable of being ran locally or even on-device, eliminating the need for LLMs entirely.

## 3 Method

An overview of our approach to generate highquality health dialogue summaries is depicted in Figure 1. For simplicity, our implementation uses the same base model for each agent. Please refer to Appendix A for the relevant prompts and Appendix C for the relevant generation parameters.

### 3.1 Summary Refinement with Text Feedback

For any conversation, we first generate initial summaries of the health dialogue using k agents. If the number of rounds is strictly greater than one, then the summaries are refined with text feedback. In this step, each agent provides text feedback on the summary that it generated. The summary feedback that we ask for looks to remove redundant information from the summary, while checking to see if there was anything in the original conversation that was not included in the initial summary. We remark that this feedback is unrestricted, since different parts of a summary may be important depending on future contexts, an aspect that makes health dialogue summarization difficult. For example, mentioning that you “went to a concert” may not typically be relevant in a health conversation summary, but may be relevant if a user is asking about how they might have contracted Covid or other infectious diseases. Then, each agent will incorporate its feedback to update its output, resulting in a refined version of the original summary. This process is then repeated until we have completed all feedback rounds. Note that in the case of one round, no feedback is generated since there is no update step (which requires at least two rounds), and instead the summaries are directly fed into the aggregation step. Importantly, during the feedback and update steps, we note that

each agent does not see the output summaries of the other agents. One example of a feedback and update step can be found in Table 19.

### 3.2 Aggregating Refined Summaries

Whereas prior research approaches this step using specialized blending modules (Zhang et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023b) or through some combination of intermediate summaries (Laskar et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022), we treat all the summaries, which may have been iteratively refined, as good candidate examples to be included in the context. More specifically, we append these refined summaries, output from the k individual agents. as candidate references the model can utilize during its final generation. We then ask the final agent to generate the final summary using all of these refined summaries as context. Essentially, these candidate references are included as in-context learning references. By incorporating siloed iterative refinement, our objective is to ensure that a diverse set of candidate references may be included in the aggregation step when generating the final summary.

### 4.2 Internal Real-World Data

To provide a realistic overview of real-world viability, we also benchmark our experiments on two internal health wellness conversation datasets, which we title “InternalA” and “InternalB”. InternalA consists of 140 health dialogues drawn from 10 different users. InternalB consists of a larger set of 536 conversations, with 161 of those contained in its test split. For our purposes, we mainly use InternalA to determine the optimal hyperparameters (i.e. number of agents and number of rounds) for each model, leaving the InternalB dataset for the main evaluation. To determine the optimal settings for each model, we conduct a grid search by benchmarking all possible combinations of agents (2,3,4) and rounds (1,2,3) on our InternalA dataset. These optimal settings are displayed in Table 1. For generation details about the InternalA dataset, please refer to Appendix B. For an accurate breakdown and description of the full results for each combination, please refer to Appendix F.

### 4.3 Models

We collect results for a suite of small LMs (less than 4B parameters) that can feasibly be ran locally or on-device. We selected the following models: Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025), Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Llama-3.2- 3B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Gemma-2- 2B-Instruct (Team et al., 2024), Gemma-3-1B- Instruct (Team et al., 2025b), Deepseek-R1-Distill- Qwen-1.5B (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and Phi-3- Mini-Instruct (Abdin et al., 2024a). In our tables, we use “IT” as a shorthand for “Instruct”, and denote the Deepseek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model as DS-Qwen-1.5B. We utilize Gemini-2.0-Flash (Team et al., 2025a)

as our LLM comparison model, as it was the latest iteration of the Gemini series (at the time) and was readily available for our use. Preliminary results on a set of larger LMs may be found in Appendix H.

## 5 Results

Winrate evaluation primarily uses Claude-3.5- Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024) as our judge, given its strong performance on winrate benchmark datasets compared with other contemporary LLMs (Tan et al., 2025). Since prior work has noted the possibility of positional bias with these LLMs, we account for this factor by running each comparison twice, swapping the position of each output in the second run (Wang et al., 2024b; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024). We count a sample as a “win” for a model if and only if our judge prefers it in both comparisons. If the preferred summary differs with the swapped comparison, we count the two summaries as “comparable”, since it was selected at least once by the judge. For brevity, results computed using automated metrics are displayed in Appendix G.

### 5.2 Open-Source Medical Datasets

On the MTS-Dialog dataset, our approach generally outperforms baseline summarization on the first test split, with the exception of the two Llama models (although only Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct is statistically significant). Otherwise, from Table 4, our refined summaries outperform baseline on all other models, with all but Qwen-2.5- 0.5B-Instruct displaying statistically significant improvements. The largest gains are seen in the Gemma-2 and Gemma-3 models, as well as Phi- 3-Mini-Instruct, with improvements of 29.00%, 13.00%, and 12.50%, respectively. The second test set is more divided: among the statistically significant improvements, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Deepseek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, and Llama-3.2- 3B-Instruct perform better in baseline summarization, while Gemma-3-1B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B- Instruct, and Phi-3-Mini-Instruct perform better

with our method. These results mirror the trends we observed in the first test split, although the average improvement of the models that perform better in baseline is notably less than the average improvement of the models that perform better with our approach (6.50% versus 17.50%). Across both test splits, Gemma-2-2B-Instruct has the highest average improvement of 27.25% when using our approach. On the other hand, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct is the worst performing model across both test splits, with its baseline summaries actually outperforming our refined summaries by 8.75%. This may in part be explained due to its prompt sensitivity, which results in the model being unable to accurately follow our proposed approach correctly, where such an issue has been noted in prior work to a degree (Arabzadeh and Clarke, 2025; Zhuo et al., 2024). Interestingly, the Deepseek-R1- Distill-Qwen-1.5B model actually exhibits different behavior on each test split, with refined summaries performing better on the first test split but baseline summaries performing better on the second test split, with both instances actually being statistically significant. ### 5.3 Viability Towards Fine-Tuning

We also conducted a case study analysis to investigate the real-world potential of our refined summaries to act as ground truth for supervised finetuning of other models. For use cases where inference latency is highly desirable, supervised finetuning could be one technique to reduce response

generation times, distilling the high quality of our refined summaries into just a single model call. We use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to generate refined summaries to act as ground truth for the InternalB training split, as it exhibited the best performance on the InternalB test split according to Table 3. On the 375 training samples, these refined summaries exhibited a winrate of 51.73%, compared to 27.47% for Gemini summaries, as well as 20.80% which were deemed comparable. The results from Table 6 are promising, with all but Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct outperforming both baseline and refined summaries. All models apart from Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct outperform Gemini (i.e. Gemini’s winrate is under 50%), with the largest improvements being Llama- 3.2-1B-Instruct at 31.68%, Gemma-2-2B-Instruct at 31.67%, and Phi-3-Mini-Instruct at 22.98%. For Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, its performance degradation can in part be attributed to the fact that it was fine-tuned on its own outputs, which prior work has shown could result in performance loss (Shumailov et al., 2024; Gillman et al., 2024).

## 6 Discussion

Across all datasets, we observe that our approach of refining summaries via textual feedback outperforms both baseline summarization and classic multiagent debate frameworks. The one exception was Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, where baseline summarization actually performed better for all but the InternalA dataset. As mentioned earlier, this may be due to the model’s prompt sensitivity. Indeed,

during our experiments, we found that Llama-3.2- 1B-Instruct sometimes tended to continue the input conversation, generating a response as if it was replying directly to the user, rather than actually performing summarization on the input dialogue. While baseline summarization performed better for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on the MTS-Dialog dataset, our refined summaries are notably better on all other datasets. Against multiagent debate, we see that our approach yields improvement on all models except for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, and in some instances Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. However, for all other models, our refined summaries still perform notably better than multiagent debate summaries. Additionally, our fine-tuning results demonstrate the viability of training other LMs on our refined summaries, illustrating our method’s potential viability as a ground truth generator for unsupervised data. Finally, we remark that our refined summaries are able to exhibit higher semantic diversity than baseline, without compromising in terms of text quality. While multiagent debate summaries can be even more diverse, this comes at the trade-off of reduced summary quality. We share detailed results and explain our findings further in Appendix E.

## 7 Conclusion

We conduct an empirical study analyzing the health conversation summarization capabilities of small LMs. We propose an approach to generate summaries by iteratively refining them using textual feedback, before merging these refined summaries to generate the final summary. Our results across both open-source and proprietary health wellness and medical conversation datasets demonstrate the viability of our method, outperforming both baseline summarization and conventional multiagent debate. Crucially, we focus primarily on small and compact LMs, and remark that our method can be run on as little as a single Macbook with 16 GB of memory, without the use of a GPU at all.

## Limitations

One limitation of our work is that we evaluated health wellness conversation summarization quality for small LMs only, i.e. models below 4B parameters. For institutions and corporations with the necessary compute requirements, we acknowledge that results on a suite of much larger models would prove beneficial. For those who are inter-

Nevertheless, these results were excluded from the main body as our work primarily focused on models that can fit on-device, given the strict guidelines and compliance regulations on where personal medical/health data can be sent to, as well as its broad applicability. This aspect is underlined by the fact that all of our experiments, apart from the fine-tuned numbers displayed in Table 6, were conducted without the use of a GPU, making our method readily accessible.

Another limitation that may arise is the additional latency overhead, which is not incurred in baseline summarization approaches. For our purposes, this constraint was not as prominent as memory constraints, as our needs only require offline summarization, prioritizing quality over inference speed. Even in worst case scenarios (4 agents, 3 rounds, no GPUs), our method incurs roughly 61.87 seconds per sample. We deem this tradeoff acceptable, particularly when working in the health wellness and medical domains, where accuracy is more highly valued than speed. Despite this, our results in Table 6 do illustrate one possible workaround: distilling our summary generation method into models via supervised fine-tuning. Then, one can utilize the fine-tuned models to perform summarization in one model call, thus eliminating the additional latency overhead introduced by our method. Realistically, we remark that this is a limitation that applies to all frameworks with multiple agents. Unlike existing approaches, however, we stress that our approach can feasibly be ran locally, and removing the dependence on LLMs entirely. We acknowledge that our approach incurs some latency, but for the purposes of our work, we were more concerned with summary quality, especially given the sensitive and decision-critical nature of the health and medical domains.

Finally, future work may also investigate the feasibility of heterogeneous models. We did not evaluate this approach due to the additional compute overhead that it requires, as our objective was instead on a method that can run even in the absence of GPU resources. Such an approach also raises additional concerns regarding model selection as well as model influence. Nevertheless, evaluating heterogeneous models may provide useful insights and comparisons with our approach, particularly in situations where GPU resources are abundant.

Ethical Considerations

We chose to conduct our open-source dataset evaluations on the MTS-Dialog and NoteChat datasets, which are open-source and publicly available. For the InternalA dataset, we note that these 140 conversations were generated synthetically, and were cleaned to ensure they do not contain personable user data or other identifiable information. As our internal data consists of health wellness conversations, the main filtering process simply removes names (data such as geographic locations were not present in our conversations). Given the nature of the task, health metrics were not removed, as that would defeat the purpose of a health wellness assistant. We note that all internal participants were made fully aware of the data collection procedure and its purposes for internal research only, and ensured consent was received before we used this data for either evaluation or fine-tuning. Additionally, our fine-tuned results on this dataset were performed privately in-house, in order to prevent data leakage and/or compromise. Due to the sensitive nature of the internal data, these datasets (presently) are unable to be released for public use. We caution that for actual real-world use, all LM deployment systems, and particularly in the health and wellness domains, should undergo further rigorous testing before being exposed for public use, in order to guard against hallucinations in the summary. At our current stage, our results and models have not yet been exposed publicly and are currently only being used for research purposes. For those that wish to adopt our approach and method, we urge that they first rigorously test and verify on their own use cases/data. As a quick remark, the Gemini-2.0-Flash model that we benchmarked our summaries against was hosted privately, rather than externally connected. We did this to guard against external data transfer, and model real-world settings where user data compliance regulations must be met.

## I Software Implementation

Our method is implemented using Python, with Ollama quantized inference used for response generation. This approach ensures that our approach can be ran viably without the use of any GPU. Finetuning was implemented in Python, using the TRL library for supervised fine-tuning, training on completions only. For these experiments, we used a single GPU node with 40 GB of memory. Although our approach utilizes multiple agents, we remark that we only require enough memory to store one model instance. Rather than instantiating a new model instance to represent each agent, we load one instance of the model and control for its generated responses with different random seeds.
